_comment: Single source of truth for competitor speed figures. See scripts/check-benchmark.mjs. Update via a measurement run, never by hand from another page.

measuredOn.note: Replaces the March 2026 figures (iPhone 15 Pro, app v1.0), which were measured five major versions ago and disagreed with three other tables on this site. See docs/SEO_AIO_PLAN_2026-08.md §11-§13.

columns.focus: tap → the note field receives focus
columns.ready: tap → the keyboard is fully presented and the app will accept a keystroke. INCLUDES every tap in the app's sequence. This is the published figure. Measured on WARM launches — see launchCondition.
columns.first_char: tap → the first character appears. Adds one human keypress on top of `ready`; recorded, not published, because that keypress ranged 0.200-0.500s across apps and belongs to the hand, not the app.

Drafts.ready_basis: FAST MODE, not the median. Runs: 0.9 / 1.55 / 1.45 / 1.383 / 1.567. The published figure is the 0.900s run on the owner's instruction to take the faster side of a bimodal set: 0.900 sits 0.48s below a cluster that itself spans only 0.18s. Every other app publishes a median. Drafts is the only app that has BOTH per-run `ready` values and a bimodal split, so it is the only one the rule can be applied to — the six apps from the full run kept only median and range. If the rule is ever applied uniformly, Drafts' median is 1.450.

Evernote.range_note: The 5.1s top of the range is one run out of five and it is real — the recording was confirmed good. Kept rather than dropped as an outlier: an app that occasionally takes five seconds to become typeable is telling you something the median hides.

otherPublishedRuns.note: Its third column is a send-inclusive total, which is a different measure and not a conflict.
Materially faster than every other run on the site. Most likely warm-start figures presented as launch times.
Splits launch / first-character / send into separate columns, so its 'launch' is a narrower measure than the canonical one.

measuredRuns.source: ScreenRecording_08112026_151315 (38.0s, 60fps, 1170x2532) — iPhone 16e, confirmed by the owner
measuredRuns.device_note: iPhone 16e (A18). An earlier version of this note inferred 'iPhone 12/13/14 class' from the 1170x2532 resolution and concluded the run used OLDER hardware than the methodology page's iPhone 15 Pro. That was wrong: the 16e shares the 14's display but carries the A18, which is a generation NEWER than the 15 Pro's A17 Pro and faster on CPU. Faster launch figures are therefore partly expected, and this run is not like-for-like with the published table either way.
deviations_from_protocol: Force quit was performed (verified frame-by-frame: the switcher card is flung upward off-screen before each relaunch), but the dwell before relaunching was 0.13-1.92s, not the documented 5 seconds.
Competitors have n=1 each; the protocol asks for 3. Only our own app has n=5.
Drafts, Bear, OneNote and Evernote were not recorded.
The 'ready' column is not recoverable from these recordings for multi-step apps — see ready_note.
measuredRuns.ready_note: Only our own app's ready time is trustworthy here (0.600s median), because its field is focused on launch — the frames show the caret in the first settled frame. For the others 'ready to type' requires taps the detector cannot model: Notion drew its sidebar at 0.883s, then needed a compose tap and a page load, with the caret appearing around 4.0s. Those elapsed times include human reaction and are not comparable.
measuredRuns.headline: Every launch figure came in far below the published table, and Google Keep (0.383s) and Apple Notes (0.433s) launched faster than our own app (0.600s). Some of the gap is hardware — the recording is on an A18, the published table on an A17 Pro — and some is app versions moving since March. But a chip generation does not explain Notion at 0.883s against a published 3.8s, or Google Keep at 0.383s against 1.5s. Those are 4x. With n=1 per competitor this does not settle the right numbers; it does say the published competitor figures are not safe to keep quoting.

measuredRuns.status: CANONICAL — promoted 2026-08-11 with owner sign-off (metric: ready/KB完全)

columns.focus: tap → the note field receives focus
columns.ready: tap → the keyboard is fully presented, i.e. the app is ready for you to type. INCLUDES any taps in the sequence.
columns.first_char: tap → the first character appears on screen. Adds one human keypress on top of `ready`.

measuredRuns.why_ready_not_first_char: `first_char` was the metric agreed on 2026-08-11, and this run measures it. On the data it turns out to be the noisier of the two: the gap between `ready` and `first_char` is the operator's keypress, and it ranged 0.200-0.500s ACROSS APPS. That 0.30s of spread belongs to the hand, not the app, and the differences being measured are 0.4-2.8s. `ready` keeps every tap the definition asked for and drops only the final keystroke, so it is the recommended published column. Both are recorded; nothing is lost by revisiting this.
measuredRuns.cross_check: Independent agreement with the earlier recording: scripts/analyze-launch-recording.py put Simple Memo's settle at 0.600s median (n=5), and this run's first_char median is also 0.600s (n=5). Two different methods, same number.
open_questions: The recordings themselves were not supplied, so these figures could not be re-derived here. Who measured what is recorded above; independent verification is not.

Precision is mixed: Simple Memo, Google Keep and one Apple Notes file are frame-accurate (multiples of 1/60s); Notion, OneNote, Evernote, Bear, Drafts and the other Apple Notes file are rounded to 0.1s. Usable, but coarser.

RESOLVED for Bear and Drafts by 2026-08-11-owner-rerecord-bear-drafts: both were re-recorded under one protocol and both figures changed (Bear 1.900 -> 0.917, Drafts 1.200 -> 1.450). The original wording follows, because the same doubt still applies to Apple Notes, Evernote, OneNote and Notion, which keep their wide ranges: "Whether force-quit + 5s dwell was followed is not visible from a table. Bear (0.7/0.8 vs 1.9-2.3) and Drafts (0.4 vs 1.2-1.5) are bimodal on `ready`, which is what a mix of cold and warm runs looks like."
Apple Notes arrived as two files (5 runs each) and is pooled to n=10 here.

measuredRuns.status: CANONICAL for Bear and Drafts only — supersedes those two apps in 2026-08-11-owner-full
measuredRuns.why: The full run left Bear (0.7-2.3s) and Drafts (0.4-1.5s) bimodal on `ready`, which is what a mix of cold and warm launches looks like. Re-recorded under one protocol to settle it.
measuredRuns.excluded: The recording opens with two further Bear launches that are not in these five: the first returns to the app switcher part-way through, and the second reaches the editor via the note list rather than +, which is a different tap sequence. Both are excluded by the owner, and the five consecutive launches after them are the adopted log.
measuredRuns.frame_precision: Variable frame rate; the owner puts boundary error at roughly +-0.02-0.05s per reading. Both apps move by far more than that.
measuredRuns.statistic_published: median, as for the other six apps. The owner proposed means (Bear 0.927, Drafts 1.370); for Bear that is 0.010s away and immaterial, for Drafts 0.080s. Drafts Run 1 (0.900s) sits well below the other four (1.383-1.567s), so the mean is pulled toward a figure four runs out of five did not reach. A mean for two apps in a column of six medians is also the per-app statistic switch this table has been trying to get rid of.
measuredRuns.headline: Bear halves: 1.900s to 0.917s, and moves from 4th to 2nd. Drafts moves the other way, 1.200s to 1.450s, and drops behind Bear. Our own lead over the nearest rival therefore narrows from 3.0x (vs Drafts) to 2.3x (vs Bear).
measuredRuns.unresolved: RESOLVED 2026-08-11 by the owner: the launches were WARM. Force quit plus a >5s dwell was performed for every run, and every relaunch was reviewed and came up warm regardless. That explains what the earlier note could not — this run landing tightly near the FAST mode of the full run rather than between the two modes — and it means the full run's bimodality was not cold-vs-warm at all. See launchCondition.
measuredRuns.exposure: RESOLVED 2026-08-11 by the owner: Apple Notes, Evernote, OneNote and Notion were recorded without incident and their figures stand as measured. An earlier version of this note called them the least trustworthy rows in the table because their ranges are wide (Evernote 2.3-5.1s, Apple Notes 1.2-2.367s, OneNote 2.2-3.3s, Notion 2.5-3.5s) and that is the shape Bear had before re-recording moved it by 2x. That inference was wrong, and retracting it changes what the ranges mean: they are not doubt about the measurement, they are how those apps behave. Evernote really does take five seconds on some warm launches. Publish the range with the median for exactly that reason.

bear_anomaly.what: Bear read 1.900s (bimodal, 0.7-0.8 and 1.9-2.3) in the full run and 0.917s (five runs inside 0.033s) on re-recording. Same device, same OS, same operator, days apart.
bear_anomaly.cause: Two different paths into a typeable state, confirmed by the owner on 2026-08-11: Bear reopens the note that was already open, keyboard up and cursor live, with no tap. The pencil button is only needed when the app comes back to the note list — which is what happens on the first launch of a session. Tap-the-pencil and resume-into-editor are not the same measurement, and a session that mixed them produces exactly the split seen: the resume runs land near 0.8s, the pencil runs near 2.0s.
bear_anomaly.status: The mechanism is CONFIRMED — it was observed directly in the re-recording, where the pencil was tapped on the first launch only and the five adopted runs all resumed. That the first session mixed the two paths is still INFERRED: those recordings were not supplied, so which path each of its runs took cannot be checked.
bear_anomaly.implication: The published 0.917s is the resume path, which is what a returning user gets and what all five measured runs did. The withdrawn 1.900s was a median across two different paths, which is not a figure for anything. A future re-run should record the path per launch — Bear is the app most sensitive to it.

readyDefinition.wording_ja: アプリアイコンをタップしてから、本文に1文字目を入力できるまで。途中で必要なタップを含む。
readyDefinition.why: This is the number the site already argues from, and it is the only one that describes the experience being sold: a thought survives or it does not. Launch time alone flatters apps that draw fast and then make you find the compose button.
readyDefinition.includes_human_reaction: Yes, and that is accepted. The tap between launch and the editor is part of what the user actually does. It adds variance, so: one operator, one session, all apps back to back — then reaction time is roughly constant across apps and the differences still belong to the apps. Do NOT mix operators or sessions within a comparison.

tapSequence.Simple Memo - for Obsidian: launch → field is already focused → type
tapSequence.Drafts: launch → new draft opens automatically (default setting) → type. If the install opens the draft list instead, tap + first and say so.
tapSequence.Bear: launch → Bear reopens the note that was already open, keyboard up → type. NO tap. The + (pencil, bottom right) was needed on the first launch of the session only; the five measured runs all resumed straight into the editor. Confirmed by the owner 2026-08-11. If a run starts from the note list instead, + is required and the launch is much slower — see measuredRuns.bear_anomaly.
tapSequence.Notion: launch → new page → wait for the page to load → type

readyDefinition.measurement_note: The caret detector finds when a cursor starts blinking, which lands on the right frame ONLY when no tap intervened. For every app with a tap in its sequence the detector's `ready` is not the defined metric — read those from the contact sheet instead, or mark the first-keystroke frame by hand. scripts/analyze-launch-recording.py flags which is which via cursor_present_at_settle.
readyDefinition.resume_behaviour: Bear is the one competitor measured on a path with no tap in it, because it reopens the note you were editing. That is genuine returning-user behaviour and the figure stands, but it is not the same path as the others: Apple Notes, Google Keep, Evernote, OneNote and Notion were each timed through their compose tap. Whether those apps also resume into an editor was not tested. If they do, their published figures include a tap a returning user would not make, and they are correspondingly too slow. Untested, and stated as untested.

launchColumnRetired: The old table carried a separate 起動速度 (app-drawn) column. This run does not measure it — it measures focus, which for a multi-step app lands after the taps, not before. Rather than carry a stale column beside fresh ones, 起動速度 is retired and `focus` published in its place.
draftsNote: Drafts has been measured three times and moved every time. The retired March table put it at 0.8s and FASTER than us, which is why /en/blog/ios-quick-capture-comparison said so in print. The 2026-08-11 full run put it at 1.200s. The re-recording produced 0.900 / 1.383 / 1.450 / 1.550 / 1.567s, and the published figure is the 0.900s fast mode (see apps.Drafts.ready_basis), which puts it level with Bear at the top of the field behind us. Publish the range with it — one run in five reached 0.900s and the rest sat near 1.45s, so the headline figure is the best of the five, not the typical one. That asymmetry is the reason the range column exists.

canonicalRunOverrides._why: canonicalRun covers six apps. These two were re-recorded after it, and their figures come from that run instead. Kept as an explicit override so no one has to diff two run blocks to find out which number is live.

bearNote: Bear is the largest single correction this table has taken: 1.900s in the full run, 0.917s on re-recording. Treat the 1.900s figure as withdrawn, not as an alternative reading — the full run mixed 0.7-0.8s and 1.9-2.3s launches and its median sat on the slow mode, while the re-recording is five runs inside a 0.033s band. It needs no fast-mode adjustment: unimodal, and its median IS its fastest run. It now ties Drafts for second at 0.9s, and the two are separated by 0.017s, which is inside the +-0.02-0.05s boundary error the owner puts on these readings.

launchCondition.protocol_performed: Force quit from the app switcher, wait more than 5 seconds, relaunch — the documented cold-start protocol, followed for every run.
launchCondition.what_actually_happened: Warm. The owner reviewed every relaunch in the recordings on 2026-08-11 and confirmed all of them came up warm despite the force quit and the dwell. On iOS 26.5.2 that sequence does not reliably evict an app from memory.
launchCondition.why_the_whole_table_is_labelled_warm: Only the Bear and Drafts re-recording was reviewed frame by frame for this, but the earlier session used the same protocol on the same device and the same OS, so the same iOS behaviour applies. Labelling two apps warm and six cold would assert a difference nothing supports.
launchCondition.why_it_matters: The methodology page claimed the opposite in print — that warm starts are faster and we publish "the more conservative cold-start figure". We were not. A comparison table is still fair when every app is warm; what is not defensible is naming a condition that was not the one measured.
launchCondition.effect_on_the_figures: None. No number moved because of this; only the label did. Warm is also the condition most users are actually in, since an app opened several times a day is rarely evicted.
